title: Tagorewui Gitanjali kala Shai-laaring: Selected Translations in Tangkhul Naga
alternate_titles: Rabindranath Tagore's Gitanjali Translated in Tangkhul Naga
Gitanjali: Song Offerings in Tangkhul Poetry
publisher: Tangkhul Cultural Council / Ukhrul Literature Circle
subject: Poetry, Mystical Devotion & Translated Classics
notes: Select lyrical translations of Rabindranath Tagore's Nobel-winning Gitanjali and patriotic poems into classical Tangkhul verse. Preserves the mystical devotion and musical metrics of the original.

front_matter.title_page: Tagorewui Gitanjali kala Shai-laaring: Selected Translations in Tangkhul Naga (1986)
front_matter.preface: Rabindranath Tagore's devotional lyrics (Gitanjali) found a naturally receptive medium in the Tangkhul lyric poetic tradition (Hao-laa). The translator rendered Tagore's yearning for the Infinite using intimate metaphors of mountain dawns, rain-bearing clouds, and traditional flute melodies.

chapters.title: Gitanjali Song 1: Thou Hast Made Me Endless (Na Ili Machamtui Sakahaisaye)
chapters.summary: Tagore's opening offering: the human soul as a frail flute through which God breathes eternal melodies.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Shai-laa 1: Na ili machamtui sakahaisaye, chichi Nawui ningkazangsai. Hi kacham kaphunga vessel hi Na khani-kathum khangareilaga kupsang-miye, kala zingsho zingsho ringkapha kathara eina kashung-sake. Hi kakat bamboo reed flute hi Na kaphung-longkhor kuppupli phungzatlaga, Awui ngalung eina thot pupupwui shai-laaring honsangserie. Nawui kathara khutwui katom eina iwui kacham lung china khangayeiwui mathatli ngapaoritlaga khongyui kapei honsange.
chapters.english_translation: Thou hast made me endless, such is thy pleasure. This frail vessel thou emptiest again and again, and fillest it ever with fresh life. This little flute of a reed thou hast carried over hills and dales, and hast breathed through it melodies eternally new. At the immortal touch of thy hands my little heart loses its limits in joy and gives birth to utterance ineffable.

vocabulary.meaning: Siphung / Pung (bamboo flute of the hills)
gentle touch, caress of divine hand

grammar_notes: Metaphorical transposition: Tagore's reed flute rendered as traditional Tangkhul 'siphung'.
Verbal frequentative: 'khani-kathum khangareilaga' (emptying repeatedly again and again).
exercises: Discuss how the flute metaphor bridges Bengali Vaishnava mysticism and Tangkhul music.
Identify the words for 'endless' and 'immortal touch'.

chapters.title: Where the Mind is Without Fear (Mangmatha Mathikhavai Ram)
chapters.summary: Tagore's universal prayer for freedom, truth, and unconstrained intellectual dignity in Tangkhul verse.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Shai-laa 35: Kachikhali ningkakhaning malei-mana, kala kakhutli phashan eina thuk-kashok-e; Kachikhali theikakhui chi mikumo pupupwui vang kacham eina ngashankahaye; Kachikhali ngalei hi shimwui wall kakat eina kashit-mashit-mana; Kachikhali tui-ngashungna lungwui kashikli eina shokhunge; Kachikhali khangachonna khut machamla phāmeikhavai otli thukzat-e; Kachikhali mashung-ngalungwui kongkhamathān china kasham custom-wui miram kashilashili mangapaorit-mana; Chithuili, I-Ava, Nawui khut eina iwui ramli ngakhur-rarsaklu!
chapters.english_translation: Where the mind is without fear and the head is held high; Where knowledge is free; Where the world has not been broken up into fragments by narrow domestic walls; Where words come out from the depth of truth; Where tireless striving stretches its arms towards perfection; Where the clear stream of reason has not lost its way into the dreary desert sand of dead habit; Into that heaven of freedom, my Father, let my country awake.
grammar_notes: Aspiration invocation: 'I-Ava, Nawui khut eina... ngakhur-rarsaklu!' (Father, let my nation awake!).
exercises: Recite 'Where the Mind is Without Fear' in Tangkhul.
How does the translator render 'narrow domestic walls'?

chapters.title: Leave This Chanting and Singing (Gitanjali Song 11)
chapters.summary: Finding God not in closed temples, but with the tiller of the soil and pathmaker breaking stones.
chapters.tangkhul_text: Shai-laa 11: Hi luishat-laa kala rosary chinawui khangayei kashikahailu! Shimkhur ngachingli khong kakat khangakhakli Na khipali reot-kasa? Nawui mik hanglu, kala theilu, Nawui Varivara chithuili maleimana! A tilling kasana luiramli ot salakha Awui ngalemli lei; A lungkhor khakka-sana shongfa shomlakha Awui ngalemli lei; A zingsho zingkhamathān kala kazingkhamik tharili athum eina li-leie, Awui chon ngaleiwui kachak eina kashung-saye. Nawui kathara chon kashikahailaga, A thada ngaleili varlu!
chapters.english_translation: Leave this chanting and singing and telling of beads! Whom dost thou worship in this lonely dark corner of a temple with doors all shut? Open thine eyes and see thy God is not before thee! He is there where the tiller is tilling the hard ground and where the pathmaker is breaking stones. He is with them in sun and in shower, and his garment is covered with dust. Put off thy holy mantle and even like him go down on the dusty soil!
grammar_notes: Agrarian elevation of labor: God resides with field tillers ('luiramli ot').
exercises: Compare Tagore's critique of ritualism with Tangkhul traditional values of honest physical labor.
Identify the words for sun and rain in verse 4.
